h1: SEO in Ludhiana for exporters selling to Lagos and Dubai
metaTitle: SEO Services in Ludhiana: Knitwear and Cycle Parts
metaDescription: Ludhiana's knitwear and cycle-part exporters get found by African and Gulf buyers. We build English export keyword sets, on a 90-day baseline guarantee.
answer: Ludhiana's export buyers sit in Lagos, Dubai, Bogotá and Dhaka, searching in English for part specifications, minimum order quantities, FOB pricing and container loads. Almost none of that appears on a typical Ludhiana manufacturer's website, which is why the enquiries go to trading companies instead. Fixing it is mostly writing down what you already tell buyers by email.
takeaways: MOQ, Incoterms, HS code, lead time and container quantity are the five facts every export buyer searches for and almost no Ludhiana site publishes.
Bicycle parts, hand tools and auto components look like one industry from inside Ludhiana. They're three unrelated keyword sets.
Knitwear buyers abroad order for a season six to nine months ahead. Your content calendar has to run on their calendar, not Punjab's.
If Amazon and Meesho outrank you for your own product, you're paying a marketplace commission to reach customers who were looking for you.

sections.h2: The buyer is abroad, and he is not searching for Ludhiana
body: Ludhiana is India's knitwear and hosiery capital, the country's bicycle and bicycle-parts hub — Hero and Avon both sit here — and a dense cluster for hand tools, fasteners, auto and tractor components and sewing machine parts. Between them they ship containers out through the inland container depot at Dhandari Kalan to Africa, the Gulf, Latin America and South Asia.

The buyer at the other end has one thing in common regardless of continent: he searches in English, and he searches for the product, not the place. "Bicycle rim manufacturer India", "acrylic sweater manufacturer OEM", "hand tools supplier bulk order", "tractor linkage parts exporter". "Ludhiana" appears in his query only occasionally, and usually only after someone has already told him the word.

Which makes "SEO company in Ludhiana ranks you #1 in Ludhiana" a service that solves a problem exporters don't have. The correct target is a global English keyword set for the product category, competing against Alibaba listings, trading companies and manufacturers in China, Vietnam and Turkey.

callout.title: The trading-company gap
callout.body: A lot of Ludhiana export enquiries end up at trading houses in Delhi and Mumbai that don't manufacture anything. They win because their websites answer the buyer's questions and yours doesn't. That is a content problem, not a capability problem, and it's the cheapest one you'll ever fix.

sections.h2: The five facts export buyers search for that your site doesn't have
body: Open ten Ludhiana manufacturer websites and you'll find company profiles, an infrastructure page, a photo of the owner with a certificate, and a contact form. Open the email your export team sends every enquiry and you'll find the actual product: quantities, terms, timelines, prices, packing.
Publish the second one. It is the entire job.

table.caption: What an overseas buyer needs before he sends an enquiry, and how he searches for it.

What to publish
Typical query shape

sections.h2: Three clusters that look like one industry from inside Ludhiana
body: From a Ludhiana address, cycles, tools and auto parts feel like neighbours. In search they share nothing — different buyers, different vocabularies, different competitors, different seasons.

**Bicycle and bicycle parts.** Buyers are distributors and assemblers, heavily in Africa and South Asia. They search by component, size and standard: rim size, freewheel teeth, hub type, frame material. Model-level and spec-level pages beat category pages every time.

**Hand tools and hardware.** Buyers are importers and retail chains, and the queries are relentlessly specific — drop-forged, chrome vanadium, DIN or ANSI standard, socket sizes, plating. This category rewards a full catalogue published as indexable pages more than any other.

**Auto, tractor and two-wheeler components.** Buyers search by vehicle application and part number. "Compatible with" and "replacement for" content is what gets found, and getting the application matrix onto crawlable pages rather than into a PDF is usually the single biggest available gain.

sections.h2: Knitwear runs on somebody else's calendar
body: The hosiery side has a scheduling problem that no amount of good writing solves if you get it wrong. Ludhiana's domestic winterwear season peaks roughly September to January. Overseas buyers for an autumn-winter range place orders far earlier — commonly six to nine months ahead, because they need sampling, approvals, production and shipping before their own retail season starts.

So a page targeting overseas AW buyers has to be live, indexed and settled well before those buyers start looking, which in practice means publishing in the first quarter of the year for a season that lands in the last. Most Ludhiana exporters publish their winter content in October, aimed squarely at buyers who finished ordering in June.

The same logic runs the other way for summer ranges and for the growing activewear and thermal segments. The rule is simple and rarely followed: publish against the buyer's ordering calendar, not against the weather outside your factory.

callout.title: A useful side effect
callout.body: Content built for overseas buying calendars — tech packs, fabric composition, GSM ranges, wash care, sampling timelines — also happens to be exactly what serious domestic B2B buyers want. One set of pages, two markets, if you write in specifications rather than adjectives.

sections.h2: Amazon and Meesho are outranking you for your own product
body: Search your own bestselling product without your brand name. There's a good chance the first page is marketplace listings, and a fair chance some of them are your own stock, sold by a distributor, at a margin you don't see.

Marketplaces are extremely hard to outrank on generic product queries. They have the domain authority, the review volume and the fresh inventory signals. Fighting them head-on for "men's woollen sweater" is a waste of a retainer.

What works is ceding the generic term and taking everything around it. Brand and model queries, which you should own outright and often don't. Bulk, wholesale and B2B modifiers, which marketplaces serve badly. Comparison and specification content, where a marketplace listing has nothing to say. And the export queries above, which no Indian marketplace competes for at all.

The economics are straightforward. A direct order keeps the marketplace commission and gives you the customer's details. That's the whole argument for owning your own search presence — more on the trade-off in [SEO versus selling on marketplaces](/compare/seo-vs-marketplace-selling).

sections.h2: Punjabi and Hindi for the half of the business that stays home
body: Not everything in Ludhiana is exported. There's a large domestic market — retail, showrooms, clinics, schools, property, restaurants, services — and there the language picture is different again.

Typed search in Punjab skews to English and Hindi more than the spoken language mix suggests, because Gurmukhi keyboard input is more friction than typing romanised Punjabi. Punjabi shows up strongly in voice search and on video. So the sensible build is a properly configured Google Business Profile, area pages using the names locals search — Model Town, Sarabha Nagar, Civil Lines, Dugri, Ferozepur Road, Gill Road — and Punjabi or Hindi content only where people genuinely search that way, rather than a full translated mirror that ages badly.

faqs.q: Should a Ludhiana exporter target local or international keywords?
faqs.a: International, almost entirely. Your buyers are in Africa, the Gulf, Latin America and South Asia, and they search the product category in English without a city name. Keep a Google Business Profile so you look like a real place, then put the budget into global product and specification queries.

faqs.q: Is SEO better than listing on Alibaba or IndiaMART?
faqs.a: It's not either-or. Marketplaces give you volume and low-quality enquiries; your own site gives you fewer, better ones and keeps the margin. The practical answer is to keep the listings running while you build search presence, then judge which channel produces qualified orders once you're tracking both properly.

faqs.q: How much do SEO services in Ludhiana cost?
faqs.a: Local agencies typically quote ₹8,000–₹30,000 a month, which funds one person's part-time attention. We start at ₹40,000 for smaller sites and ₹75,000 for a full retainer, ex-GST, month-to-month after the first quarter with 30 days' notice.

faqs.q: Do we need a separate website for exports and domestic sales?
faqs.a: Usually no — one domain with two clearly separated sections works better, because both benefit from the same authority. What you do need is separate navigation, separate content and separate tracking, so an export buyer never lands on a page written for a Punjabi retail customer.

faqs.q: Will publishing our MOQ and prices help competitors?
faqs.a: Your competitors already know your MOQ. Buyers don't, and the missing information is why they contact someone else. Publish ranges and terms rather than exact quotes if you're nervous, but publish something. Silence loses more orders than transparency ever has.

faqs.q: How long does it take to see export enquiries?
faqs.a: Impressions on target product queries generally move in 6–10 weeks. Real enquiries follow the buyer's sourcing cycle, so 3–5 months is a realistic window, and longer for seasonal apparel where you may be publishing for a buying window two quarters away.
